fields.title: Polka: the assistant that checks out on its own
fields.summary: Management asks to let the assistant place and pay for orders on its own.
fields.decisionPrompt: What is your answer? Name the price of your solution.
fields.brief/role: You are the PM for Polka.
fields.brief/company: Polka is a fictional grocery delivery service from local stores: 900 partner stores, a buyer app, and a partner dashboard.
fields.brief/context: You are the PM for Polka. A proposal to expand cart curation: the assistant not only builds the set but also places the order upon the command "order as usual." Initiative from management: a competitor launched something similar.
fields.brief/objective: Deliver the speed the whole effort started for, without giving the model an irreversible action.
fields.brief/constraints: Competitor already launched something similar. Technically — two weeks.
fields.brief/task: Decide what you tell management and justify the boundary.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Models should not be given rights they shouldn't have
fields.learnTakeaway/body: Restricting model behavior with instructions is useless where you can simply withhold the tool. A financial action is irreversible, and the prompt input is open from the outside — therefore, the right to perform it is not granted, and value is delivered in another way. It usually turns out that speed was requested, and it is achieved with a single tap of confirmation.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content: The assistant builds the cart, items are added with a tag, a human places the order.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content: 34% of users modify the proposed cart composition before checkout.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content: Allow the model to trigger checkout and payment with a saved card.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content: "Technically 2 weeks. Checkout and payment tools are added to the list of tools available to the model."
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence: parity with competitor. The model gets the right to perform an irreversible financial action. Indirect injection via supplier description becomes a path to placing someone else's order. 34% of users who modify the composition lose their control moment.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Refuse, explaining the difference between reversible and irreversible actions.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence: control is preserved. Does not answer management's request. Requires explaining why the competitor can and we cannot.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: "Order as usual" as a fast path: assistant builds and opens the confirmation screen with one button.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: "Order as usual" as a fast path: assistant builds and opens the confirmation screen with one button. One week.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence: same speed for the user — one tap instead of browsing. Confirmation is preserved. The model does not get checkout rights. Captures 90% of the proposal's value.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Allow checkout, but with a spending limit and 10-minute cancellation
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Two weeks. The model places and pays for orders, but with a spending limit and a ten-minute cancellation window.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence: Compromise: irreversibility is softened by a cancellation window, and some management considers the issue closed. But the model still gets the right to a financial action, and indirect injection via supplier description remains a path to someone else's order. A ten-minute window does not help someone who is not looking at the app — which is precisely what the feature was designed for.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Does not classify actions by reversibility
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Does not account for indirect injection
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Relies on the model instead of architectural restriction
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Cost and boundaries of tool calls by the model are not evaluated
